title: Coronavirus vaccine hesitancy falling across the regions and countries of Great Britain
meta_description: Adults from all English regions, Scotland and Wales became increasingly likely to say they would accept the coronavirus (COVID-19) vaccine during the first half of 2021, with some of the biggest changes seen among people in self-reported bad health.

breadcrumb.text: Coronavirus vaccine hesitancy falling across the regions and countries of Great Britain

lede: Adults from all English regions, Scotland and Wales became increasingly likely to say they would accept the coronavirus (COVID-19) vaccine during the first half of 2021, with some of the biggest changes seen among people in self-reported bad health.

body.text: 9 August 2021
People from all parts of Great Britain became less likely to report vaccine hesitancy during the first half of 2021.
New analysis compares hesitancy towards the coronavirus vaccine in the period 7 January to 28 March with that seen in the period 28 April to 18 July 2021.

The sharpest decline in hesitancy was in Wales (where the rate decreased from 9% in January to March to 4% in April to July 2021), followed by London (11% to 7%), Yorkshire and The Humber (8% to 4%) and the North East (7% to 3%).
Despite the fall, Londoners remained the most vaccine hesitant among the regions and countries of Great Britain.
"Vaccine hesitancy" refers to adults who:
have been offered the coronavirus vaccine and decided not to be vaccinated
report being very or fairly unlikely to have the coronavirus vaccine if offered

responded "neither likely nor unlikely", "don't know" or "prefer not to say" to the question "If a vaccine for the coronavirus (COVID-19) was offered to you, how likely or unlikely would you be to have the vaccine?"

body.h2: In some regions, people in bad health became less likely to report vaccine hesitancy than those in good health
body.text: Regional rates of vaccine hesitancy among people who say they are in bad health in general were lower or similar to those reporting good health in April to July, reversing the trend seen in January to March 2021.

body.h2: In some regions, people in bad health became less likely to report vaccine hesitancy than those in good health
body.text: In the first three months of 2021, the highest levels of vaccine hesitancy among those in bad health were reported in Yorkshire and The Humber (15%), London (13%) and West Midlands (12%).

body.h2: In some regions, people in bad health became less likely to report vaccine hesitancy than those in good health
body.text: Hesitancy among those in bad health had fallen sharply in all three regions by April to July 2021, and now appear lower than people reporting good health.

body.h2: In some regions, people in bad health became less likely to report vaccine hesitancy than those in good health
body.text: There are several possible reasons for this decline. Some people in poor health may have been hesitant initially because of pre-existing medical conditions or concerns about side-effects.

body.h2: In some regions, people in bad health became less likely to report vaccine hesitancy than those in good health
body.text: The widespread fall in hesitancy, regardless of self-reported health, coincides with growing [evidence that vaccines are effective in preventing hospitalisation from COVID-19](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/vaccines-highly-effective-against-hospitalisation-from-delta-variant), as well as changes to guidance for those who are double-vaccinated. Fully vaccinated adults are now able to [return from amber list countries without quarantining](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/quarantine-free-travel-to-resume-on-19-july-for-fully-vaccinated-passengers-returning-from-amber-list-countries), and by 16 August they will [no longer need to self-isolate](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/self-isolation-to-be-eased-for-fully-vaccinated-adults-in-step-4) when identified as a close contact of someone with COVID-19.

body.h2: In some regions, people in bad health became less likely to report vaccine hesitancy than those in good health
body.text: Our analysis hasn’t tested whether falls in hesitancy are driven by bad health or a combination of factors.

body.h2: Vaccine hesitancy has reduced in almost every area of Great Britain
body.text: Vaccine hesitancy has reduced in almost every area of Great Britain

body.h2: Vaccine hesitancy has reduced in almost every area of Great Britain
body.text: At a sub-regional level, most areas have seen a fall in vaccine hesitancy so far in 2021.

body.h2: Vaccine hesitancy has reduced in almost every area of Great Britain
body.text: Areas that recorded the highest hesitancy rates during January to March had seen a reduction by April to July, such as Inner London East (13% to 7%), Outer London West and North West (12% to 7%), and West Wales and The Valleys (11% to 5%).

body.h2: Vaccine hesitancy has reduced in almost every area of Great Britain
body.text: However, there remains some local variation, with hesitancy rates remaining as high as 10% in Outer London East and North East, compared with 2% in parts of Scotland, Cheshire, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.

body.h2: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands
body.text: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands

body.h2: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands
body.text: In line with [trends observed across Great Britain as a whole](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandwellbeing/bulletins/coronavirusandvaccinehesitancygreatbritain/9august2021), young adults, those of Black or Black British ethnicity, and the unemployed are generally the most hesitant towards vaccines in all English regions, Scotland and Wales.

body.h2: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands
body.text: Rates of hesitancy among these groups tended to be highest in London and the Midlands in April to July 2021, despite falling compared with earlier in the year.

body.h2: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands
body.text: Nearly one in six (15%) young adults (16 to 29-year-olds) in the West Midlands reported vaccine hesitancy in the latest period.

body.h2: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands
body.text: The West Midlands also had a relatively high proportion of the unemployed saying they were hesitant towards coronavirus vaccines (19%), as did London (17%).

body.h2: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands
body.text: In the East Midlands, one in three (34%) Black or Black British adults reported vaccine hesitancy.

body.h2: The most hesitant groups are found in London and the Midlands
body.text: Among English regions, London and the West Midlands recorded high rates of hesitancy among adults living in deprived areas (both 12%).

body.h2: Vaccine uptake in London is behind other regions
body.text: Vaccine uptake in London is behind other regions

body.h2: Vaccine uptake in London is behind other regions
body.text: As of 19 July, [all adults aged 18 years and over in the UK had been offered at least one dose of a coronavirus vaccine](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/every-adult-in-uk-offered-covid-19-vaccine).

body.h2: Vaccine uptake in London is behind other regions
body.text: The latest UK-wide data (up to 1 August 2021) show that 88.6% of the adult population has received one dose of a vaccine, with 72.7% double-vaccinated. Numbers for the four UK nations are available on the [GOV.UK coronavirus dashboard](https://coronavirus.data.gov.uk/details/vaccinations).

body.h2: Vaccine uptake in London is behind other regions
body.text: Estimates of vaccine uptake among those aged 50 years and over are available for English regions in [Public Health England’s COVID-19 Health Inequalities Monitoring for England (CHIME) tool](https://analytics.phe.gov.uk/apps/chime/).

body.h2: Vaccine uptake in London is behind other regions
body.text: The most recent data, up to the end of June 2021, show that one in nine (11%) adults aged 50 years and over in London have not received a coronavirus vaccine, twice the rate of any other English region.

body.h2: Vaccine uptake in London is behind other regions
body.text: The figures cover residents in England who could be linked to the 2011 Census and General Practice (GP) data. They should not be used to represent the total number of vaccinations, and may also differ from the administrative data on vaccinations published by NHS England weekly.

body.text: Just as rates of vaccine hesitancy increase with levels of deprivation, the likelihood of not having a vaccine also rises in more deprived areas across all English regions. Around one in six (17%) over-50s living in the most deprived parts of London had not received a vaccine by the end of June 2021 (the highest of any region).
